title: Resources
text:
Material produced by our group that may be useful beyond our own research.





Cryosphere maps
Poster maps of the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets, showing surface ice velocity over shaded topography, drainage regions, the sea-ice edge and place names. The collection also includes maps of the Northern Hemisphere and Antarctic ice sheets at the Last Glacial Maximum, as well as vintage-style maps with expedition routes and wildlife. All maps are generated from published datasets with Julia and CairoMakie. The website provides interactive versions and printable posters in A0 format.
 Interactive maps and posters  fesmc/cryosphere-maps

title: AWI Earth System Complexity
text:
Earth System Complexity
The Earth System Complexity group at AWI is focused on understanding interactions between large-scale components of the Earth — the ice sheets and ocean circulation, boreal forest and permafrost. We strive to increase our understanding of the relevant processes driving dynamics within these systems on long timescales, using numerical models and paleo data analysis.

title: For students
text: We welcome students who are interested in doing a Bachelor’s or Master’s thesis with our group. Most thesis projects are based on numerical modeling or on the analysis of model output and observations. Each project addresses a current research question and is supervised by a scientist who works with the models and data involved.

title: For students
text:
What we do
Our group investigates how the cryosphere interacts with the rest of the climate system, on timescales from decades to glacial cycles. Our research covers the following topics:

Ice sheets and glaciers. We simulate the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets, as well as past ice sheets, with the ice-sheet model Yelmo.
Snowpack and surface mass balance. We model how snow accumulates, melts and refreezes with the snowpack model Chion.jl. These processes determine the surface mass balance of ice sheets and glaciers.
Mountain glaciers. We study the evolution of mountain glaciers at the regional scale and their response to climate change.
Climate–cryosphere interactions. We use coupled models such as CLIMBER-X to study the feedbacks between ice sheets, atmosphere and ocean.
AMOC and the Southern Ocean. We investigate the stability of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) and the role of the Southern Ocean in the climate system, including their response to meltwater from the ice sheets.

title: For students
text:
What we look for
Most projects involve programming, mainly in Julia and Fortran. Experience with these languages is helpful, but not required. More important is an interest in physical processes and a willingness to learn technical tools, such as running models on a computing cluster and analyzing large datasets. We welcome students from physics, mathematics, geosciences, meteorology, oceanography, computer science and related fields.
A member of our group typically acts as co-supervisor of the thesis. The supervision arrangement differs between universities, so it should be determined early in the project.

title: For students
text:
Potential topics
The topics below are examples of projects we are currently offering. Most can be adapted to the level of the thesis and to your interests. If none of them fits, we are also happy to discuss your own ideas. For a specific topic, please contact the person listed. For general questions, write to Alexander Robinson.



A machine-learning surface mass balance model MSc
Physically based surface mass balance (SMB) models are computationally expensive for long simulations or large ensembles. Machine-learning (ML) models trained on their output offer a computationally efficient alternative. In this project, you will extend an existing ML-based SMB model, for example by adding predictors, testing other model architectures or applying it to new regions. Some familiarity with ML methods is helpful.
Contact: Nils Bochow
machine learning surface mass balance emulation




Albedo parameterizations for a surface mass balance model BSc MSc
Surface albedo determines how much shortwave radiation is absorbed by snow and ice, and thus how much energy is available for melt. In this project, you will develop and test albedo parameterizations for the snowpack model Chion.jl, which calculates the surface mass balance (SMB) of ice sheets and glaciers. The parameterizations will be constrained with satellite observations (e.g., MODIS). Depending on your interests, this can include simple machine-learning models trained on the observations.
Contact: Nils Bochow
Chion.jl surface mass balance albedo machine learning MODIS remote sensing




Edge states of the Greenland ice sheet MSc
The Greenland ice sheet (GrIS) has multiple stable states for the same climate. These are separated by unstable states, so-called edge states, that mark the boundary between their basins of attraction. In this project, you will use the ice-sheet model Yelmo to locate edge states of the GrIS with numerical methods such as edge tracking. The results indicate how far the ice sheet can be perturbed before it no longer recovers. The project is purely model based.
Contact: Nils Bochow
Yelmo Greenland tipping points dynamical systems




Effect of extreme events on surface mass balance BSc MSc
Heat waves and other extreme weather events can cause large melt anomalies, such as the melt events over the Greenland ice sheet in 2012 and 2019. In this project, you will use the snowpack model Chion.jl to quantify how such events affect the surface mass balance of the Greenland ice sheet or of mountain glaciers. Possible questions include how much of the total mass loss is caused by a few extreme events, and whether changes in their frequency or changes in the mean climate dominate future mass loss.
Contact: Nils Bochow
Chion.jl surface mass balance extreme events Greenland glaciers

title: Research
text: Our group investigates how ice sheets, glaciers and snow interact with the atmosphere and ocean, on timescales from decades to glacial cycles. This work depends on numerical models that are fast enough to simulate many thousands of years or to run large ensembles, while still representing the relevant physical processes. For this reason, a large part of our effort goes into developing such models and making them openly available.

title: Research
text:
Model development

Yelmo ice-sheet model
Yelmo is a thermomechanical ice-sheet model that can be applied to any ice sheet, from present-day Greenland and Antarctica to the ice sheets of past glacial periods. It solves for ice flow with a choice of approximations to the Stokes equations (e.g., the shallow-ice, shallow-shelf and depth-integrated viscosity approximations). We use Yelmo to study ice-sheet tipping points, paleo ice-sheet evolution and long-term sea-level rise. Yelmo runs as a stand-alone model or coupled to CLIMBER-X, and a Julia version (Yelmo.jl) is under development.
Robinson, A., Alvarez-Solas, J., Montoya, M., Goelzer, H., Greve, R., and Ritz, C.: Description and validation of the ice-sheet model Yelmo (version 1.0), Geosci. Model Dev., 13, 2805–2823, doi.org/10.5194/gmd-13-2805-2020, 2020.
 fesmc/yelmo


CLIMBER-X Earth system model
CLIMBER-X is a fast Earth system model (fESM) that couples a statistical-dynamical atmosphere to a three-dimensional ocean, sea ice, a land surface with dynamic vegetation and an interactive carbon cycle. It simulates on the order of 10,000 years per day, which makes it suitable for glacial cycles and for large ensembles of future projections. We use CLIMBER-X to study the stability of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC), variability in the Southern Ocean and the long-term response of the ice sheets to warming.
Willeit, M., Ganopolski, A., Robinson, A., and Edwards, N. R.: The Earth system model CLIMBER-X v1.0 – Part 1: Climate model description and validation, Geosci. Model Dev., 15, 5905–5948, doi.org/10.5194/gmd-15-5905-2022, 2022.
 cxesmc/climber-x

title: Research
text:
Fast Earth system modeling community
Yelmo and CLIMBER-X are part of a wider effort to develop fESMs as open, modular software. The Fast Earth System Modeling Community hosts Yelmo together with related components, such as the snowpack model Chion.jl, models of glacial isostatic adjustment and basal hydrology, and tools for preparing input data. CLIMBER-X is maintained by the CLIMBER-X Earth System Modelling Community. Each component can be run stand-alone or coupled within a fESM, which allows individual processes to be tested before they are used in long coupled simulations.
